tasks.locator: Materials and Method › Subjects, 1st paragraph (p. 514); Substances and Dosing, 1st paragraph (p. 514); Study Design, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (pp. 514-515)
tasks.extracted: Double-blind, placebo-controlled, within-person study of 16 volunteers (12 men and 4 women, aged 21 to 39) in four counterbalanced conditions at least 14 days apart: placebo then placebo, citalopram then placebo, placebo then MDMA, citalopram then MDMA. Citalopram 40 mg (or saline) was infused over 90 minutes, then MDMA 1.5 mg/kg (mean 100 mg, SD 10) was taken by mouth, and ratings were made 120 minutes after MDMA. Six volunteers had tried recreational drugs before: two ecstasy, three a hallucinogen and one both. Editors' count: 3 of the 16 had tried ecstasy and 13 had not.

tasks.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph (pp. 515-516); Figure 1 (p. 516); Table 1 (p. 517)
tasks.extracted: MDMA raised all three altered-state scales against placebo (Rao R(3,12)=7.25, P<.005) and citalopram pretreatment lowered them (pretreatment by treatment: oceanic boundlessness F(1,15)=22.47, anxious ego dissolution F(1,15)=23.04, visionary restructuralization F(1,15)=12.80). Item clusters, percent of maximum, MDMA alone against citalopram then MDMA: positive basic mood 40.1 against 16.4, derealization 32.7 against 12.6, thought disorder 24.8 against 8.6, changed meaning of percepts 37.3 against 14.1; of the 15 item clusters, MDMA significantly raised 13, and citalopram significantly lowered 10 of those 13 but not frightening derealization, synesthesia or facilitated recollection. Editors' calculation from the printed means: the ten lowered clusters fell by about 55 to 80 percent.

tasks.locator: Results, last paragraph (p. 516); Figure 2 (p. 518); Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 517) and the paragraph beginning 'Non-specific untoward effects' (pp. 518-519)
tasks.extracted: On the mood scales, citalopram lowered the MDMA-induced rises in self-confidence (P<.04) and extroversion (P<.01) to the level of citalopram alone, and efficiency-activation (P<.03); the fall in heightened mood did not reach significance (P=.06), and the rises in emotional excitability and sensitivity were not lowered at all. Citalopram alone lowered some scale scores against placebo, which the authors put down mostly to its side effects (fatigue, headache and nausea; nausea in 6 of 16).

tasks.locator: Results, 1st paragraph (p. 515); Discussion, paragraph beginning 'Another interesting finding' and the continuation of the paragraph beginning 'Non-specific untoward effects' (p. 519)
tasks.extracted: MDMA's subjective effect lasted a mean of 3 hours; after citalopram it was markedly reduced but lasted a mean of 5 hours, stated without a method, spread or test. No blood concentrations were taken. The authors put the lowering at about 60 percent and note that all received the same 40 mg whatever their weight, with no correlation between dose per kilogram and the size of the lowering; in a pilot, two people given 60 or 80 mg of citalopram had MDMA's effects blocked to a degree comparable with 40 mg.

tasks.locator: Materials and Methods › Subjects, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Study Design, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 955)
tasks.extracted: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover in 12 healthy men (mean age 24; all extensive CYP2D6 metabolizers; MDMA taken on at least 5 earlier occasions). Two 3-day sessions 15 days apart: paroxetine 20 mg a day or placebo on days 1 to 3, with MDMA 100 mg on day 3, 3 hours after that day's capsule. A 13th man withdrew after two paroxetine doses (insomnia, restlessness, anxiety) and never took MDMA.

tasks.locator: Table 1 (p. 957); Results › Physiological Effects and Subjective Effects (p. 957); Figs. 1 to 3 (pp. 958-960)
tasks.extracted: Paroxetine lowered MDMA's effects: peak systolic pressure 12 mm Hg lower (Emax F=22.20, P=0.001), diastolic 5 mm Hg and heart rate 14 beats/min lower, pupil widening from 3.33 to 1.23 mm (F=70.35, P<0.001), temperature rise 0.3 C lower (P=0.041); ARCI euphoria scale (morphine-benzedrine group) peak 7.27 to 4; VESSPA anxiety 5.55 to 2.7, sociability 3.0 to 0.58, activity 5.91 to 1.21; visual-analogue 'stimulated', 'high', 'any effect', 'good effects' and 'liking' lower (all P=0.003 or less at peak). By Table 1 the diastolic area (P=0.613) and peak (P=0.213) and the heart-rate area (P=0.093) were not significant.

tasks.extracted: MDMA with paroxetine against placebo (n=12): peak 246.62 against 212.72 ug/L and area to 21 hours 2572.21 against 2115.26 ug x h/L, both P<0.01; HMMA peak 97.88 against 193.14 and area 1189.47 against 1923.32, half-life 13.10 against 9.54 hours (all P<0.01); MDMA half-life 8.34 against 7.88 hours. The paper's own text gives MDMA 22 (exposure) and 16% (peak) higher and HMMA 39 (exposure) and 49% (peak) lower. Editors' calculation from the printed means: HMMA exposure -38%.

tasks.locator: Abstract (p. 954); Table 1 and Results › Subjective Effects (p. 957); Discussion, final paragraph (pp. 961-962)
tasks.extracted: Ratings of bad effects, fear, and depression or sadness did not change significantly with paroxetine, and no hallucinations, psychotic symptoms or serious adverse events were seen. The authors write that the marked decrease in positive effects may lead to higher MDMA doses (they give people with depression who take SSRIs as an example) and so to potentially life-threatening toxicity; no extra MDMA was given in the study, so this is their inference. The abstract gives the rise in MDMA level as 30%, a figure taken in the Discussion from an earlier 7-man analysis; the trial's own figures are 16% (peak) and 22% (exposure to 21 hours).
tasks.quote: could lead users to take higher doses of MDMA

tasks.locator: Discussion, 5th and 6th paragraphs (p. 529)
tasks.extracted: The authors write that a single recreational dose of MDMA inhibits CYP2D6 rapidly and completely whereas several prescription doses of paroxetine are needed, that citalopram and paroxetine block the positive effects of MDMA, and that people taking an SSRI together with multiple doses of MDMA should know that the metabolism of both substances is compromised, with a possible increase in the risk of acute adverse effects already reported for poor metabolizers. The reference given for people taking SSRIs to change MDMA's effects is a rat study. No SSRI was given with MDMA in this study.

tasks.locator: Materials and Methods › Subjects, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 526); Drugs, 1st paragraph; Study Design, 1st to 4th paragraphs (pp. 526-527)
tasks.extracted: Fifteen healthy men (mean age 26, range 19 to 33; on average 26 previous MDMA experiences) who were extensive CYP2D6 metabolizers at screening, recruited by word of mouth and paid. Open, fixed-order design: session 1 (control, dextromethorphan 30 mg with caffeine 100 mg), then at least 3 days later session 2 (MDMA 1.5 mg/kg, 75 to 100 mg, with caffeine and dextromethorphan 30 mg at 4 hours and later); the dextromethorphan schedule was 4, 24, 48, 72, 96 and 168 hours in the first 3 men and 4, 24, 72, 96, 168 and 240 hours in the other 12, because the ratio had not recovered by 168 hours; results pooled. No placebo MDMA session.

tasks.locator: Table 1 (p. 527); Results › Plasma Concentrations of DEX, DOR, MM, HM, and MDMA Pharmacokinetics and Pharmacodynamic Effects, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 528)
tasks.extracted: Plasma probe drug after MDMA against the control session (Table 1, n=15): dextromethorphan peak 3.5 to 29.7 ng/mL (SDs 3.6 and 18.5) and area over 8 hours 15.7 to 149.1; dextrorphan peak 464.6 to 31.9 and area 1877.1 to 179.1; 3-hydroxymorphinan peak 164.1 to 16.6 and area 764.2 to 97.5 (all P<0.05); 3-methoxymorphinan not significantly changed. The authors say the dextromethorphan peak and area increased approximately 10-fold. MDMA peak 194.3 ng/mL (SD 30.9) at 2.0 hours (SD 1.0). Editors' calculation from the printed means: 8.5-fold for the peak and 9.5-fold for the area.

tasks.locator: Results › Urinary DEX/DOR MR and CYP2D6 Recovery Half-Life, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Figure 2
tasks.extracted: The urinary dextromethorphan to dextrorphan ratio rose from 0.0061 (SD 0.0056) to 0.4322 (SD 0.2848), which the authors call almost 100-fold; 67% of the men had a value above 0.3, the cut-off for assigning the poor-metabolizer phenotype, after MDMA; no correlation of the ratio with urine pH (r=0.049) or creatinine (r=0.214). Recovery fitted one exponential curve: rate constant 0.016 (SD 0.005) per hour, recovery half-life 46.6 hours (SD 11.8), r2=0.791. Editors' calculation: the ratio of the printed means is 71-fold, and 67% of 15 men is 10 men.

tasks.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph (pp. 528-529); 3rd paragraph (p. 529)
tasks.extracted: The ratio had not recovered fully to its basal level at 10 days; the half-life corrected for MDMA's own residence time is 37.4 hours (SD 11.6), and the authors think it underestimates recovery because activity had not recovered even at 10 days; a two-phase fit gives 103.0 hours (SD 70.3), corrected 93.7 (SD 70.4), though variability and few time points question the biphasic model. Editors' reading: the first probe dose after MDMA was given 4 hours after it, when MDMA was near its peak, so competition for the enzyme cannot be separated from its inactivation in the early hours.

tasks.locator: Table 1 (p. 527); Results › Plasma Concentrations of DEX, DOR, MM, HM, and MDMA Pharmacokinetics and Pharmacodynamic Effects, 1st paragraph (p. 528); Results › Urinary DEX/DOR MR and CYP2D6 Recovery Half-Life, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 528)
tasks.extracted: In 15 men, a single MDMA dose of 1.5 mg/kg raised the exposure to the CYP2D6 probe drug dextromethorphan from 15.7 to 149.1 (area over 8 hours) and its peak from 3.5 to 29.7 ng/mL, lowered the product dextrorphan from 464.6 to 31.9 ng/mL at peak, and raised the urinary probe-drug to product ratio from 0.0061 to 0.4322; the recovery half-life was 46.6 hours (SD 11.8) on one fit, and the ratio had not fully recovered at 10 days.

tasks.locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph (p. 529)
tasks.extracted: The authors recall their own earlier study in which MDMA concentrations were increased beyond what accumulation predicts when a second dose was taken 24 hours later. They also write that people who use MDMA are known to take on average more than 1 pill per session (1.8 to 2.9 pills on average, up to 6 to 7 depending on the type of person, citing their reference 36, which was not read) and that many binge for several days, and infer, without having given a second dose, that a second dose taken up to a week later would give higher plasma concentrations and, they add, a higher risk of acute toxicity. No second dose, concentration-effect measure or toxicity outcome was studied here (editors' reading).

tasks.locator: Research letter, 3rd paragraph (the summary above the text counted as the 1st; begins 'The UK National Teratology Information Service')
tasks.extracted: The UK National Teratology Information Service followed up 136 pregnancies (one pair of twins) with ecstasy exposure from January 1989 to June 1998; there were 302 enquiries, of which 31 (10%) were not yet completed and 135 (45%) were lost to follow-up because the enquirer could no longer identify the patient or she did not return to the surgery.

tasks.locator: Research letter, 5th and 6th paragraphs (begin '74 pregnant women reported' and '127 women')
tasks.extracted: 74 women reported ecstasy only and 62 ecstasy with other drugs of abuse (amphetamine 37, cocaine 20, cannabis 16, alcohol 13, LSD nine, other 13); acute toxicity from ecstasy in two mothers. 127 women (71 ecstasy alone, 56 with other drugs) were exposed in the first trimester, two in the first and second, two in the second and one in the third; four were exposed to several drugs throughout pregnancy.

tasks.locator: Research letter, 7th and 8th paragraphs (begin '11 pregnancies resulted in miscarriage' and 'There were 78 liveborn infants'); summary above the text; Table (Malformations reported after exposure of fetus to ecstasy and other drugs of abuse)
tasks.extracted: 11 pregnancies ended in miscarriage (8%, within the expected range) and 48 in elective termination (35%, higher than the UK average; one after prenatal diagnosis of malformations); no necropsy data on the other aborted fetuses; by subtraction (editors' arithmetic) the other 77 pregnancies gave the 78 live-born infants, one pair being twins. 78 live-born infants: 66 normal and 12 with congenital anomalies, 15.4% (95% CI 8.2 to 25.4), described as significantly higher than an expected incidence of 2 to 3%, with no test or P value given; the summary calls this a possible association with a significantly increased risk of congenital defects; the table lists 13 anomaly findings (12 live-born, plus one terminated fetus with absent upper limbs), among them a toe under its neighbour, plagiocephaly, pyloric stenosis, ptosis, pigmentation of a thigh and clicking hips. No source is given for the expected incidence.
tasks.quote: may be associated with a significantly increased risk of congenital defects

tasks.locator: Research letter, 9th and 10th paragraphs (begin 'Eight infants were born prematurely' and 'No adverse effects were observed in the sex ratio')
tasks.extracted: Eight infants were born prematurely (25 to 36 weeks, including twins at 25 weeks; two fetal distress cases thought unrelated to ecstasy); one neonatal death in an infant of a mother who took ecstasy, heroin and methadone throughout pregnancy; no adverse effect on sex ratio; birthweights within the expected range for term infants, with only three under 2.5 kg.

tasks.locator: Research letter, 11th and 12th paragraphs (begin 'There were three female infants with talipes' and 'The spontaneous incidence of congenital heart disease'); summary above the text
tasks.extracted: Three female infants had talipes (38 per 1000, CI 8 to 109, against an expected 1 per 1000; the letter says idiopathic talipes is male-predominant 3 to 1 in the UK); two infants had congenital heart disease, ventricular septal defects (26 per 1000, CI 3.0 to 90.0, against an expected 5 to 10 per 1000). The authors say the small series has insufficient statistical power to confirm a causal relation with any particular anomaly but consider the data important. Editors' reading of the table: the three infants with talipes were in the ecstasy-only group, and both infants with a ventricular septal defect had other drug exposure.

tasks.source_read: PDF Dubois_2015_AlcoholCannabisCrashRisk.pdf (the journal's accepted manuscript), text extracted once with pdftotext -layout; tables and figures checked on rendered pages
tasks.extracted: FARS drivers of cars, sport-utility vehicles and light trucks aged 20 or older in fatal crashes, 1991–2008, with a blood alcohol test and at least one blood drug test: 150,010 of 722,220 eligible (about one in five, editors' calculation); groups 87,280 alcohol- and THC-free, 53,992 alcohol only, 3,387 THC only, 4,347 both (these add to 149,006; 1,004 more with two or three THC-positive tests were left out of the main analyses). Outcome: a police-recorded potentially unsafe driver action (proxy for responsibility), so the comparison is among drivers already in fatal crashes. THC is a yes/no blood marker of unstated analyte with no concentration, dose or timing; the authors note THC can remain in the blood for hours or days and that FARS does not say why THC was present. The paper reports no rating of how impaired drivers felt. Appendix 1 (comparison of tested and untested drivers) is not in the manuscript.

tasks.extracted: The paper describes the effect of alcohol and cannabis together as appearing greater than that of either alone, generally additive (seven sources cited) or possibly synergistic (six), with some research finding no additive effect (three); at low alcohol with small cannabis amounts it calls the results inconsistent: one on-road study found no significant difference in a driving proficiency test against drug-free driving, although visual search at intersections fell by 3% (p = .041), while another found severe impairment with the combination and only minor to moderate impairment with each alone. Second-hand: these studies were not read for this library.

tasks.extracted: Re-analysis of the nine studies of Asbridge et al. and nine of Li et al.: a culpability odds ratio estimates the increase in risk of a culpable crash, higher than the increase in all crashes (a simulation shows the culpability estimator biased upwards); re-extraction changed four of nine Asbridge odds ratios by more than 10%, all downwards (Blows 7.2 to 2.6; Terhune 4.4 to 1.7). Fig 4, read by eye from an enlarged crop (approximate): Asbridge nine studies 1.92 reported, about 1.59 with corrected counts, 1.40 with the adjusted culpability estimator, 1.31 with adjusted estimates from the underlying studies and about 1.25 with both; Li nine studies 2.66 reported, about 1.55 with adjusted estimates. The Discussion (p. 8) says the revised value for the Asbridge studies lies between 1.22 and 1.36. The correction leaves standard errors unreduced (footnote 1); after corrected counts alone the intervals still contain the original 1.92 and 2.66.

tasks.locator: Results › Risk of bias assessment, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 6, continued p. 8); Discussion › Alternative interpretations of the results, 1st to 4th paragraphs; Conclusions, 1st paragraph (p. 10)
tasks.extracted: Included studies scored 4.11 of 5 on quality of information on use (excluded studies 2.16); poor measures such as urine tests bias towards no effect, while non-response among roadside controls probably inflates odds ratios; drivers who use cannabis may drive when they judge impairment low (understating risk) and may share traits with higher crash risk such as high speed and drink-driving (overstating it). The authors conclude that acute intoxication is associated with a statistically significant increase in crash risk of low to moderate magnitude and that remaining selection effects may complicate a causal reading. The paper words positive tests as intoxication; no included study measured impairment.

tasks.extracted: Secondary analysis of the Euro-DEN Plus Registry (22 emergency departments in 14 countries, 18 contributing patients; 17,371 presentations; 2,349 with GHB/GBL; 467 without ethanol data excluded; 1,273 with other drugs excluded; 183 and 426 analysed). GHB/GBL and ethanol status by report of the patient or companions, the attending physician or toxicology at the physician's discretion (done in 38 patients, 6.2%, finding GHB/GBL in 28.9%); no amounts, timing or product; each centre's principal investigator adjudicated cases with no central review; univariable tests only, about 33 comparisons without correction; six centres supply 93% of patients (editors' arithmetic from Table 1: two London centres 297, two Oslo centres 209). Not included: patients managed before reaching an emergency department. The author notes that low frequencies of some features may hide differences and that unreported co-ingested drugs cannot be excluded. Fig 1 and Table 1 checked on the rendered pages.

tasks.locator: Results › Decision rules, 1st paragraph; Figure 2
tasks.extracted: Figure 2, decision rules: in the presence of a serotonergic agent, serotonin toxicity is yes if (1) spontaneous clonus; (2) inducible clonus with agitation or diaphoresis; (3) ocular clonus with agitation or diaphoresis; (4) tremor with hyperreflexia; or (5) hypertonic with a temperature above 38 C and ocular or inducible clonus; otherwise no. Seven variables were needed: spontaneous, inducible and ocular clonus, agitation, diaphoresis, tremor and hyperreflexia. Rule 5 was added although the classification-tree analysis did not select it, because clonus and hyperreflexia are often not demonstrable in severe rigidity; the life-threatening cases were not in the learning dataset of SSRI-alone overdoses, because they occur with combinations of serotonergic agents.

tasks.locator: Table 1, parts a to c
tasks.extracted: Table 1a, Hunter rule against the toxicologist's diagnosis: not diagnosed and not flagged 1785; not diagnosed but flagged 62; diagnosed but not flagged 27; diagnosed and flagged 145; row totals 1847 and 172, column totals 1812 and 207, 2019 in the table; printed sensitivity 84% and specificity 97%. Table 1b, Sternbach's criteria as the reference: 1951, 67, 64, 140; printed 69% and 97%. Table 1c, treatment with a 5-HT2A antagonist as the reference: 1991, 124, 24, 83; printed 78% and 94%. The grand total of Table 1b is printed as 222. Editors' calculation (Wilson 95% intervals; the paper gives none): sensitivity 145/172 = 84.3% (78.1 to 89.0); specificity 1785/1847 = 96.6% (95.7 to 97.4); positive predictive value 145/207 = 70.0% (63.5 to 75.9); negative predictive value 1785/1812 = 98.5% (97.8 to 99.0).

tasks.locator: Table 2; Results › Decision rules, 3rd paragraph (continued from p. 639)
tasks.extracted: Table 2, Sternbach's criteria against the toxicologist's diagnosis in the same records: not diagnosed and not flagged 1772; not diagnosed but flagged 75; diagnosed but not flagged 43; diagnosed and flagged 129; printed sensitivity 75% and specificity 96%; the printed column totals (1833 and 186) do not match the cells. The paper gives no interval and no test of the difference from the Hunter rule. Editors' calculation: 129/172 = 75.0% (68.0 to 80.9); 1772/1847 = 95.9% (94.9 to 96.7); column totals from the cells 1815 and 204; positive predictive value 129/204 = 63.2%.

tasks.locator: Introduction, last paragraph (p. 637); Methods, 1st paragraph (p. 637); Methods › Derivation dataset and Test dataset (p. 638); Results, 1st paragraph and SSRI-alone overdoses, 1st paragraph (p. 638)
tasks.extracted: The Hunter Area Toxicology Service is a regional toxicology unit; every overdose presentation and admission is entered prospectively into a clinical database by two trained staff who were blind to the hypotheses. Of 9960 admissions between 13 January 1987 and 22 November 2002, 2222 involved at least one serotonergic drug taken in overdose; this test dataset had no exclusions and includes the derivation dataset. Derivation dataset: 473 admissions with a single SSRI, after excluding 9 with two SSRIs and any with a tricyclic antidepressant, MAOI, venlafaxine, nefazodone, lithium or an anti-serotonergic drug taken as well. Of the 473, 73 (15.4%, 95%CI 12.3–19.0) had a diagnosis of serotonin toxicity made by a clinical toxicologist, 70 (14.8%, 95%CI 11.7–18.4) met Sternbach's criteria and 44 (9.3%, 95%CI 6.8–12.3) were treated with a 5-HT2A antagonist. The tree analysis was done in the SSRI-alone dataset; the rules were tested on the complete dataset. The paper reports no ages, sex, drugs or amounts.

tasks.locator: Results › Life-threatening serotonin toxicity (single paragraph)
tasks.extracted: Life-threatening cases were those intubated and ventilated. Forty-two patients were intubated for a decreased Glasgow Coma Score or for decontamination; six were intubated solely for worsening serotonin toxicity. All six had a high fever and multiple features of serotonin toxicity. Progressive rigidity compromising respiratory function was the precipitating event; the preceding signs were a high fever (above 38.5 C) and increasing, particularly truncal, rigidity and peripheral hypertonicity. Editors' calculation: 6 of 2222 admissions = 0.27%.

tasks.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph (continues in the right-hand column, from the words The arbitrary approach taken)
tasks.extracted: The authors state that the approach was arbitrary and was mandated by the lack of a gold standard for defining clinically significant serotonin toxicity, which is a spectrum and not a discrete syndrome; they therefore used the diagnosis made by a clinical toxicologist as the standard and compared it with Sternbach's criteria and with the use of treatment.
tasks.quote: mandated by the lack of a gold standard

tasks.locator: Discussion, paragraph beginning Although mydriasis occurred commonly (top of the left-hand column); Discussion, last paragraph (beginning The decision rules will need to be validated)
tasks.extracted: Mydriasis occurred in 31.6% of patients and tachycardia in 40%, but both also occur with anticholinergic and other drug toxicity (tachycardia is common in drug overdose in general), so the authors call them unlikely to be good discriminators of serotonergic excess from other toxidromes. The authors acknowledge the arbitrary nature of certain decisions in developing the criteria. They state that the decision rules will need to be validated in other settings, including other toxicology treatment centres, emergency departments and psychiatric units, and studied prospectively in people taking toxic and therapeutic amounts of serotonergic drugs.

tasks.locator: Introduction, paragraph beginning Serotonin excess is best thought of as a spectrum (right-hand column)
tasks.extracted: The authors write that serotonin excess is best thought of as a spectrum of toxicity rather than a defined clinical entity with clear prognostic importance, and so call it serotonin toxicity; that it results from an increase in serotonin in the synapses of the central nervous system, so is a concentration-dependent toxicity that can develop in any individual and not an idiosyncratic reaction; and that it can be thought of as a triad of autonomic signs, neuromuscular changes and altered mental status.

tasks.locator: Opening paragraph; Definition and epidemiology, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: The review calls the serotonin syndrome a potentially life-threatening adverse drug reaction, a predictable consequence of excess serotonin stimulation of receptors, with clinical manifestations from barely perceptible to lethal. It is often described as a triad of mental-status changes, autonomic hyperactivity and neuromuscular abnormalities, but not all are present in every person; signs range from tremor and diarrhoea in mild cases to delirium, neuromuscular rigidity and hyperthermia in life-threatening cases; mild symptoms may be easily overlooked.

tasks.locator: Definition and epidemiology, paragraph beginning To better delineate the signs and symptoms (p. 1114); Diagnosis, 2nd paragraph (p. 1115)
tasks.extracted: The review describes its source as the clinical findings in 2222 consecutive cases of self-poisoning with serotonergic drugs from a toxicology registry, compared with the gold standard of a medical toxicologist's diagnosis, and says its preferred decision rules are simpler, more sensitive (84 percent against 75 percent) and more specific (97 percent against 96 percent) than the original criteria. It does not say that the figures come from one unit or that the rules were derived in part of the same records, gives no intervals, and does not mention the source paper's statement that no gold standard exists.

tasks.locator: What is serotonin syndrome?, 1st paragraph; How does it present?, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: The review describes serotonin syndrome, also called serotonin toxicity, as a drug-induced cluster of dose-related adverse effects due to increased serotonin in the central nervous system, covering a spectrum from mild to severe. It says toxicity starts within hours of ingesting the drugs and that the classic triad is neuromuscular excitation (clonus, hyperreflexia, myoclonus, rigidity), autonomic excitation (hyperthermia, tachycardia) and altered mental state (agitation, confusion).

tasks.locator: How do we diagnose it?, 2nd paragraph (beginning Some pathognomonic features)
tasks.extracted: The review calls generalised clonus (inducible, spontaneous, ocular) the classic feature and the key component of the Hunter criteria, which it says have been validated and can be used to confirm moderate or severe toxicity; the only source cited for this statement is the derivation paper (reference 13). It describes spontaneous clonus as rhythmic, large muscle contractions, often triggered by minor movements or vibrations and easily brought out with ankle dorsiflexion, and ocular clonus as fine or coarse oscillations of gaze in all directions.

tasks.locator: Introduction, paragraph beginning Serotonin syndrome is a drug-induced toxic state
tasks.extracted: The review says people with serotonin syndrome from illicit drugs such as ecstasy usually reach emergency departments with more advanced symptoms, because some of the early, mild signs are generally seen by many people who use ecstasy as part of normal drug reactions; it cites one earlier review for this and gives no data. It describes the typical picture as agitation or hypervigilance with tremor and exaggerated reflexes, with muscle spasms starting in the lower limbs and becoming generalised, then fever, sweating, dilated pupils, rapid heart rate and rapid breathing, and fixed rigidity in severe cases.

tasks.locator: Abstract
tasks.extracted: The abstract describes four deaths following ingestion of moclobemide and MDMA, says the probable cause of death in each was serotonin syndrome as a result of an interaction between the two drugs, and infers a purpose for taking moclobemide because none of the four had been prescribed it. The pathologists' stated cause in each case, in the case descriptions, is combined accidental poisoning with the two drugs, and the Discussion says it is not known why the victims combined the substances.

tasks.locator: Method (reference ranges; the single paragraph begins on p. 365); Case 1, Case 2, Case 3 (p. 366); Case 4 (begins at the foot of p. 366)
tasks.extracted: Reference ranges quoted in the Method: MDMA in blood 0.1–0.35 mg/l; moclobemide 1.5–2.5 mg/l. Case 1: woman aged 18, unknown quantity of street ecstasy, next morning suddenly confused, convulsed, lost consciousness and stopped breathing; no temperature taken; blood MDMA 1.6 mg/l, moclobemide 2.3 mg/l; alcohol in blood and urine; amphetamines in urine. Case 2: man aged 23 found dead after a confused state, with two kinds of white tablets that both contained MDMA; blood MDMA 2.0 mg/l, moclobemide 2.1 mg/l, dextromethorphan 1.1 mg/l (quoted range 0.01–0.04), plus morphine, amphetamine, cyclizine and several benzodiazepines; the pathologist counted dextromethorphan as contributing. Case 3: man aged 18 who had used amphetamine-type drugs for years, suddenly confused, rolled about on the floor, collapsed; body temperature of the deceased 43.2 C; blood MDMA 1.7 mg/l, amphetamine 0.15 mg/l, moclobemide 7.9 mg/l, cannabis in blood and alcohol in urine. Case 4: man aged 19 who had taken 10 ecstasy tablets, unconscious with breathing difficulties, died in hospital; no temperature; blood MDMA 2.1 mg/l, moclobemide 6.5 mg/l, cannabis, MDA and lidocaine. In all four the pathologist concluded combined accidental poisoning with MDMA and moclobemide. No clonus, reflexes, tone or tremor is recorded for any. Editors' calculation: the four MDMA concentrations are 4.6, 5.7, 4.9 and 6.0 times the upper end of the quoted MDMA range (0.35 mg/l); moclobemide 0.9, 0.8, 3.2 and 2.6 times the upper end of its range (2.5 mg/l).

tasks.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph; paragraph beginning Moclobemide had not been prescribed; paragraph beginning It is not known why the victims combined these substances; last paragraph
tasks.extracted: The authors say that, to their knowledge, no fatal cases of this combination had been reported before; that history and clinical observations were limited in most cases, but the mode of death in each was consistent with a serotonin syndrome as Sternbach described it; that moclobemide had not been prescribed for any of the victims and was present at maximum therapeutic concentration in cases 1 and 2 and in moderate overdose in cases 3 and 4; that it is not known why the victims combined the substances; that the only known link between the cases is the region, with cases 1 and 2 close in time; that in case 2 moclobemide could also have slowed the breakdown of dextromethorphan; and that the risk of death is high if another drug affecting serotonin release, especially an MAO inhibitor, is taken together with MDMA, a statement given without a rate or a comparison.

tasks.locator: Results › High risk, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 651, right-hand column; the 2nd paragraph ends at the top of the left-hand column of p. 652)
tasks.extracted: The review places ecstasy taken with MAOI antidepressants (phenelzine, tranylcypromine), other MAOIs and the reversible inhibitor moclobemide in the high-risk group, as likely to lead to serious increases in serotonin. It says cases of serotonin syndrome from ecstasy with phenelzine have been reported as early as 1987 (two older case reports, not read here) and that ecstasy with moclobemide can give rise to fatalities, a handful of cases being documented (the Finnish series read here); it says further evidence that moclobemide increases the likelihood of severe serotonin syndrome with ecstasy comes from animal studies.

tasks.locator: Results › High risk, paragraph beginning In a recent Australian study (left-hand column)
tasks.extracted: Approximately one in 25 people in a recent Australian study of people who use ecstasy reported deliberately combining ecstasy and moclobemide (a technical report by two of the review's authors; the review gives no sample size, recruitment method or time frame); the same research is said to have found that deliberately taking antidepressants with ecstasy went with a greater likelihood of reporting muscle rigidity, nystagmus, dizziness, headache and profuse sweating.

tasks.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph (begins in the left-hand column and ends in the right-hand column)
tasks.extracted: The authors say that since the late 1980s only a handful of case reports of ecstasy-induced harm that fit the diagnostic criteria for serotonin syndrome have been described; that the incidence of ecstasy-related fatalities seems low compared with the likely frequency of use, but the extent of acute non-fatal harm is harder to estimate because less serious cases are not usually published; and that fatalities from serotonin syndrome with ecstasy overdose alone are relatively rare, while the potential for serious toxicity is greater when ecstasy is taken together with other serotonergic drugs or substances.

tasks.locator: Implicated drugs, 1st paragraph (begins on p. 435 and ends at the top of the left-hand column of p. 436)
tasks.extracted: The review states that illicit stimulants such as MDMA, if combined with MAOIs (including moclobemide), also cause fatalities because they act as serotonin releasers; that serotonin releasers with MAOIs are the only other combination, besides MAOIs with serotonin reuptake inhibitors, able to cause serotonin toxicity of a severe and potentially fatal degree; that several unpublished cases of MAOI and releaser combinations are known to the author; and that a recent case series of four deaths has been reported by Vuori (the paper read here).

tasks.locator: Definition and epidemiology, paragraph beginning A striking number of drugs and drug combinations
tasks.extracted: The review says that MAOIs that are irreversible or nonselective or that inhibit monoamine oxidase subtype A are strongly associated with severe cases of the syndrome, especially when used in combination with meperidine, dextromethorphan, SSRIs or MDMA, and cites other papers for this sentence; the Finnish series is not among the review's references.

tasks.locator: Abstract
tasks.extracted: The abstract gives the aim as bringing together the risk of serotonin syndrome from taking ecstasy with other serotonergic substances into a hierarchy for doctors, from an extensive online database search. Findings: substances that inhibit serotonin reuptake are less likely to lead to life-threatening elevations in serotonin when taken with ecstasy; high doses or repeated use of stimulants such as methamphetamine and cocaine with ecstasy increase the risk, as does pharmaceutical amphetamine with ecstasy; serotonin precursors also influence the course; and substances that inhibit monoamine oxidase are most likely to lead to serious increases in serotonin with ecstasy.

tasks.locator: Method, single paragraph (right-hand column)
tasks.extracted: A review of peer-reviewed and grey literature up to 2006 using Embase, CINAHL, Medline and PubMed, with search terms that included but were not limited to those listed (a minority from ecstasy-related websites). Substances were categorized as less, intermediate or high risk with ecstasy according to the proportion of agreement between studies; comment on the methodological quality of each study was not made; national experts were consulted when appropriate. No inclusion criteria and no count of records found or used are given.

tasks.locator: Results › Less risk, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (p. 650; the 3rd ends at the top of the left-hand column of p. 651); Table 1 (p. 651)
tasks.extracted: Substances that inhibit serotonin reuptake (SSRIs, the SNRI venlafaxine, tricyclic antidepressants, the opioid analgesics tramadol and dextromethorphan, and antihistamines) are said not to be likely to raise serotonin to life-threatening levels with ecstasy, because they compete with MDMA at the serotonin receptor site and so diminish its effects (the wording is the review's; reuptake inhibitors act at the transporter). Controlled studies are said to find that the physiological and subjective effects of ecstasy are substantially reduced in participants given citalopram; animal experiments are said to show that some SSRIs block MDMA-induced serotonin release; whether SSRIs protect against MDMA's long-lasting neurotoxic effects in humans is said to be yet to be determined. Bupropion is said to be devoid of clinically significant serotonergic effects. Table 1 sets out the groups: less, intermediate, high and unknown risk.

tasks.locator: Results › Intermediate risk, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (left-hand column) and 4th and 5th paragraphs, on 5-HTP and L-tryptophan (right-hand column)
tasks.extracted: Because severity depends on the type and quantity of substance, ecstasy, a potent releaser of serotonin, taken with other releasers or precursors is said to be likely to carry a greater risk of serious serotonin syndrome; high doses or repeated use of ecstasy and its analogues are said to intensify serotonin release; serious serotonergic symptoms are said to have been reported more often when ecstasy is used with amphetamine and cocaine (a source not read here). Dexamphetamine and methylphenidate are called relatively potent serotonin releasers (Table 1 prints ethylphenidate), as is methamphetamine. For 5-HTP the review cites a review that found no reported human cases of serotonin syndrome, with deaths from overdose in animals, and says its use with ecstasy is in theory likely to precipitate the syndrome; for L-tryptophan it says the risk is likely to increase if it is combined with ecstasy, especially if used beforehand.

tasks.locator: Results › Unknown risk, four paragraphs (beginning The herbal extract Saint John's wort, Lysergic acid, Anti-migraine drugs and Relatively little is known about the mechanism of action of lithium)
tasks.extracted: St John's wort, LSD, the anti-migraine drugs dihydroergotamine and bromocriptine, and lithium have serotonergic properties or have been implicated in serotonin syndrome, but the review says that whether they carry clinically relevant serotonergic potency, or can cause life-threatening symptoms, has not been established; the anti-migraine risk is presented as more of a theoretical concern.

tasks.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph (begins in the left-hand column and ends in the right-hand column)
tasks.extracted: The authors say that since the late 1980s only a handful of case reports of ecstasy-induced harm that fit the diagnostic criteria for serotonin syndrome have been described; that ecstasy-related fatalities seem low in incidence compared with the likely frequency of use, but non-fatal harm is harder to estimate because less serious cases are not usually published; and that fatalities from serotonin syndrome with ecstasy overdose alone are relatively rare, while the potential for serious toxicity is greater when ecstasy is used together with other serotonergic drugs or substances.

tasks.locator: Discussion, paragraph beginning Emerging evidence that a range of serotonergic pharmaceutical drugs and supplements (right-hand column)
tasks.extracted: The review says there is emerging evidence that serotonergic medicines and supplements are deliberately combined with ecstasy to achieve a specific effect, in some cases with serious consequences, and that anecdotal information from ecstasy-related websites suggests this is not uncommon; the medicines named are SSRIs, MAOIs, 5-HTP, St John's wort and pharmaceutical amphetamine. It adds that people who use ecstasy tend to use other serotonergic illicit drugs on the same occasions, with alcohol, cannabis, amphetamine and cocaine frequently combined with ecstasy.

tasks.locator: Implicated drugs, paragraphs beginning Overall, there is a strong association and Also, a recent review of the literature
tasks.extracted: The review by Gillman calls tramadol and venlafaxine anomalous, because their estimated potency as reuptake inhibitors suggests they should not be a risk, and says there is evidence they also act as serotonin releasers, which may account for the discrepancy. It says a recent review of the literature shows that, of the releasers, amphetamine is relatively potent and a risk, whereas methylphenidate is a weak releaser. Gillman's Table 1 lists amphetamine and MDMA as serotonin releasers.

tasks.locator: Abstract (last sentences)
tasks.extracted: The abstract says the phenylpiperidine series opioids pethidine (meperidine), tramadol, methadone and dextromethorphan, and propoxyphene, appear to be weak serotonin reuptake inhibitors and have all been involved in serotonin toxicity reactions with MAOIs (including some fatalities), and that morphine, codeine, oxycodone and buprenorphine are known not to be reuptake inhibitors and do not precipitate serotonin toxicity with MAOIs. It also says that only combinations of serotonergic drugs acting by different mechanisms can raise serotonin to a life-threatening level, and that the combination that most commonly does so is an MAOI with any reuptake inhibitor.

tasks.locator: Table 1 and its caption; Table 2
tasks.extracted: Table 2, serotonin transporter binding (Ki, nM; a lower value means higher potency; the caption says the values come from different sources and species and cannot be compared directly) and reports with MAOIs: morphine 500 000 (other references) and >100 000 (Codd), none; codeine, buprenorphine and oxycodone >100 000, none; tramadol 760 and 528, definite, and possible fatalities; dextromethorphan 23, definite; pethidine 413 weak, anomalous, definite, and some fatalities; pentazocine, no reports known; fentanyl, uncertain, one case of serotonin toxicity and one possible death reported; remifentanil, no case or death reported; methadone 270 and 14.1, no reports known, but unlikely. The Table 1 caption says fatalities from serotonin toxicity involving analgesics have been with pethidine, tramadol and dextromethorphan and, possibly, fentanyl.

tasks.locator: Implicated drugs, paragraph beginning Overall, there is a strong association
tasks.extracted: The reviewer states that binding affinities at the serotonin transporter of less than 1 nM are invariably associated with the ability to precipitate toxicity with MAOIs and that potencies in the 1–10 nM range are borderline; that tramadol and venlafaxine are anomalous because their estimated potency suggests they should not be a risk, and that there is evidence they also act as serotonin releasers; and that pethidine, a very weak reuptake inhibitor, shows a large discrepancy that could possibly be accounted for by serotonin releasing properties, although there is no direct evidence. Editors' reading: every Table 2 value for pethidine, tramadol, methadone and dextromethorphan (14.1 to 760 nM) is above the 1–10 nM borderline range.

tasks.locator: Implicated drugs, paragraph beginning The early drugs that were involved (begins at the foot of p. 436 and continues on p. 437)
tasks.extracted: The reviewer says the early drugs involved in these interactions (pethidine and imipramine) are weak reuptake inhibitors and, because there is a dose–effect relationship, usually fail to produce a reaction. He describes a 1968 experiment (Evans-Prosser) in which 15 patients were given injections of pethidine, morphine or water in graduated doses in hospital, in blind random order (study condition: top single pethidine dose 75 mg, morphine 7.5 mg); none had serotonergic symptoms; reflexes and clonus were not examined, only pulse and arterial pressure. He reads this as confirming that weak reuptake inhibitors like pethidine are sometimes capable of precipitating toxicity, but only in susceptible individuals or with particularly large doses. He says the complete list of references on serotonin toxicity and analgesics, located through a search of the listed papers and standard databases (approximately 40), is on his website; that pethidine has undoubtedly caused a number of severe reactions and some fatalities, and the other reuptake-inhibiting analgesics also some fatalities; that a small series using usual therapeutic doses may lead to a false sense of security because the dose–effect relationship is not sufficiently appreciated; and that differences in cytochrome P450 enzymes produce 20–50-fold variations in serum levels between patients.

tasks.locator: Implicated drugs, paragraphs beginning The limited available clinical and experimental data agree, Details of all cases involving analgesics and There are a few individual case reports (right-hand column)
tasks.extracted: The reviewer says the limited clinical and experimental data agree that morphine analogues (morphine, codeine, oxycodone, buprenorphine) are not reuptake inhibitors, none precipitates serotonin toxicity with MAOIs, and there are no reports with them; that the phenylpiperidine opioids (pethidine, tramadol, methadone, fentanyl and congeners, dextromethorphan, propoxyphene) are probably all borderline, weak reuptake inhibitors, implicated in multiple reports that are almost certainly serotonin toxicity as judged by a subjective interpretation of the old case reports; that about 40 cases involving analgesics are in his updated review; and that all the opioid analgesics with serotonergic effects have been involved in serotonin toxicity reports but none of the drugs without reuptake-inhibiting capacity have. For fentanyl he judges one case report with a fatality (cardiac surgery in a patient on MAOIs) probably a result of serotonin toxicity and another possibly an unrecognised case, says there is a question mark over fentanyl, that it has probably been used in many unreported cases with MAOIs without a problem, and that there is insufficient basis for an accurate estimate of the risk.

tasks.locator: Conclusion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
tasks.extracted: The conclusion says morphine, codeine, oxycodone and buprenorphine are known not to be reuptake inhibitors and do not precipitate serotonin toxicity with MAOIs, and that pethidine, tramadol, dextromethorphan and methadone definitely are weak reuptake inhibitors and may infrequently precipitate dose-dependent serotonin toxicity with any type of MAOI, but perhaps only in large doses or susceptible individuals. The ability to estimate the risk is said to be compromised by a lack of systematically recorded clinical data and of precise potency data; for propoxyphene, pentazocine, fentanyl, remifentanil and congeners there are no reuptake affinity data, so interpolation and the presence or absence of clinical reports are used. The reviewer writes that the level of risk with known serotonergic opioids is probably low, but its unpredictable and serious nature makes it difficult to form judgments, and that any reaction is dose-dependent.

tasks.locator: Implicated drugs, paragraph beginning The early drugs that were involved, sentences on fatalities (p. 437); reference list, entries 14, 31, 48, 53, 57 to 60, 63, 64, 69 and 70 (pp. 440–441)
tasks.extracted: The sentences naming fatalities cite six papers for pethidine and six for the other reuptake-inhibiting analgesics, one paper appearing in both lists. The printed reference list shows reference 31 to be a study of fatal hyperthermia in rabbits, reference 60 to be titled as a paper on malignant hyperthermia with hypocalcaemia, reference 53 to be titled MAO inhibitors and coronary artery surgery: a patient death, and reference 14 (the 1968 experiment) to be titled The use of pethidine and morphine in the presence of monoamine oxidase inhibitors. Editors' reading of the titles of the eleven papers: where a title names an MAOI it is iproniazid, phenelzine (also under its brand name Nardil) or, in the rabbit study, pargyline; none names moclobemide. Editors' count from the printed reference list: of the eleven different papers cited for fatalities, nine date from 1955 to 1971 and two from 1986 and 1992.

tasks.locator: Opening paragraph (final sentence, p. 1112); reference 4 (pp. 1119–1120)
tasks.extracted: The review states that the death of an 18-year-old patient in New York City more than 20 years earlier resulted from coadministration of meperidine (pethidine) and phenelzine (an MAOI) and calls it the most widely recognized example of this preventable condition. Its only support is reference 4, a 1988 article in the same journal whose title refers to the case itself; the review does not discuss how the cause of death was established.

tasks.locator: Definition and epidemiology, paragraph beginning A striking number of drugs and drug combinations (p. 1113); Table 1 (p. 1114)
tasks.extracted: The review says MAOIs that are irreversible or nonselective or that inhibit monoamine oxidase subtype A are strongly associated with severe cases of the syndrome, especially when used in combination with meperidine, dextromethorphan, SSRIs or MDMA. Its Table 1 lists the analgesics meperidine, fentanyl, tramadol and pentazocine among drugs associated with the syndrome, and phenelzine and meperidine as the first of seven combinations listed under drug interactions associated with severe serotonin syndrome, with no counts for any pair.

tasks.locator: Box 1 and its footnote; How do we diagnose it?, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: Box 1 lists drugs associated with moderate to severe serotonin toxicity: among MAOIs, phenelzine, tranylcypromine, iproniazid, isocarboxazid, moclobemide, linezolid and methylene blue; and, among serotonin reuptake inhibitors, the opioid analgesics pethidine, tramadol, fentanyl and dextromethorphan. The footnote says severe toxicity generally involves a combination of agents from different drug classes. The text calls the serotonergic actions of drugs not marketed as serotonergic, such as tramadol and fentanyl, a trap for the unwary.

tasks.locator: How can we prevent it?, 2nd paragraph (beginning An awareness of drugs with potent serotonergic effects)
tasks.extracted: The review says it is apparent from systematic reviews of case reports (six references) that nearly all severe serotonin syndromes involve a monoamine oxidase inhibitor, and that the relatively small number of these can easily be committed to memory. Editors' count from the reference list: four of the six cited reviews are by Gillman, one of them the 2005 review on opioids and MAOIs.
